lesson.title: The Eighteenth Amendment: Prohibition as Progressive Reform
lesson.summary: Ratified in January 1919 and taking effect in January 1920, the Eighteenth Amendment banned the manufacture, sale, and transportation of intoxicating liquor nationwide, the culmination of decades of temperance activism that many Progressives folded into their broader project of using government to fix social ills.
lesson.body:
The movement to restrict or ban alcohol in the United States long predated the Progressive Era. The temperance movement had organized since well before the Civil War, and it gained powerful institutional voices in the late nineteenth century through the Woman's Christian Temperance Union, founded in 1874, and especially the Anti-Saloon League, founded in 1893, which became one of the most effective single-issue lobbying organizations in American political history. These groups argued that alcohol, and the saloon culture surrounding it, caused poverty, domestic abuse, and the corruption of urban political machines, since saloons often served as informal headquarters for the very machine politics that Progressive reformers were simultaneously trying to dismantle.

Prohibition fit comfortably within the broader logic of the Progressive Era even though it drew on much older moral and religious arguments than reforms like trust-busting or food safety regulation. Progressives shared a general confidence that organized public policy could improve social conditions and eliminate sources of poverty and vice, and many came to see alcohol consumption through that same lens, as a social problem amenable to a legislative solution rather than simply a matter of individual choice. The movement drew disproportionate strength from rural and small-town Protestant America, and it often carried an undercurrent of hostility toward the immigrant, urban, working-class culture in which saloons played a central social role, a tension that ran through Progressivism more broadly given the era's mixed record on immigration and inclusion.

The temperance campaign gained decisive momentum during the First World War. Wartime arguments for conserving grain used in brewing and distilling, combined with a surge of anti-German sentiment that fell partly on America's many German-descended brewers, gave prohibition supporters a patriotic argument that helped push the amendment through Congress in 1917. It was ratified by the required number of states by January 1919 and, under a provision written into the amendment itself, took effect one year later, in January 1920. Congress then passed the Volstead Act, formally the National Prohibition Act, to define enforcement details and the legal threshold for what counted as an intoxicating beverage.

Prohibition proved extraordinarily difficult to enforce. It fueled a massive underground market for illegal alcohol, enriched organized crime networks that smuggled and distributed liquor, and lost the federal and state governments significant tax revenue at exactly the moment the Great Depression made that revenue more necessary. Public support collapsed over the 1920s and into the early 1930s, and in 1933 the Twenty-First Amendment repealed the Eighteenth outright, the only time in American history a constitutional amendment has been fully reversed. Even so, the Eighteenth Amendment remains a central example of the Progressive Era's willingness to use the most powerful tool available, the Constitution itself, to try to legislate a moral and social transformation of the country.
